column2: Quick. What's eighty-five squared?
Seven thousand two hundred twenty-five. Eight times nine is seventy-two. Then write twenty-five.
If that took you longer than four seconds, here's why. School teaches multiplying on paper. For this one, that's two rows of digits and three carries, built up from the small end.
On paper that's fine, because the paper remembers the rows. In your head, you have to hold both rows while you add them.
The trick holds one number. Seventy-two.
And it rests on a picture. If you ever forget the trick, the picture gives it back. So every trick here comes with its picture, and with problems for you to try.
Here's that trick on a smaller number. Thirty-five squared. Look at the number in front of the five. Three.
Multiply it by the next number up. Three times four is twelve.
Then write twenty-five after it. One thousand two hundred twenty-five.
But why the next number up? Why three times four, and not three times three?
Thirty-five squared is the area of a square, thirty-five on each side. Slice a strip off its side, five wide.
Now turn the strip, and lay it along the top.
The square has become a rectangle. Five narrower, so thirty wide. Five taller, so forty tall. And the end of the strip sticks out. A small square, five by five.
Thirty by forty is three times four, in hundreds. Twelve hundred.
And the small square is the twenty-five. Twelve hundred plus twenty-five. Twelve, then twenty-five. The next number comes in because thirty-five sits halfway between thirty and forty.
Your turn. Whenever you want more time, pause the video. What's twenty-five squared?
Two times three is six. Then twenty-five. Six hundred twenty-five.
Now past a hundred, where the number in front is ten. What's a hundred and five squared?
Ten times eleven is a hundred and ten. Then twenty-five. Eleven thousand and twenty-five.
It works for every whole number that ends in five, because the picture never changes. Whatever is in front, the strip is five wide and the corner is twenty-five.
In letters, call the number in front n. The square is n times the next number, in hundreds. Plus twenty-five.
It's only as easy as that one multiplication, though. A hundred thirty-five squared needs thirteen times fourteen. We'll come back for that.
Most products don't end in five. Take twenty-three times forty-six. Before anything else, round first. Twenty times fifty is a thousand. So the answer is somewhere near a thousand.
Now draw it. A rectangle, twenty-three by forty-six. Its area is the answer.
Break each number into parts. Twenty and three. Forty and six. The rectangle falls into four pieces.
Take the big piece, twenty by forty. Two times four is eight. But eight what? Eighty, eight hundred, or eight thousand?
Eight hundred. Twenty times four is eighty already, so twenty times forty has to be ten times that. Tens times tens are hundreds.
So leave the zeros out while you multiply, and put them back by asking how big the piece has to be. That's how twenty times fifty came to a thousand. Two times five is ten, in hundreds.
The other three go the same way. Twenty times six, a hundred twenty. Three times forty, a hundred twenty again, by coincidence. Three times six, eighteen.
Four easy multiplications. Now there are four numbers to hold while you add them.
Four numbers is a lot to hold. So don't hold them. Keep one running total, and add each piece the moment you have it.
Block, strip, strip, corner. Twenty times forty, eight hundred. Twenty times six, nine hundred twenty. Three times forty, one thousand forty. Three times six, one thousand fifty-eight.
Between steps, you only ever held one number. And every total on the way was a floor. The answer could only go up from it.
Your turn. Six times forty-three?
Six forties, two hundred forty. Six threes, eighteen. Two hundred fifty-eight.
And the one we left. It has four pieces, so pause if you like. Thirteen times fourteen?
Ten tens, a hundred. Ten fours, a hundred forty. Three tens, a hundred seventy. Three fours, a hundred eighty-two. So a hundred thirty-five squared is eighteen thousand two hundred twenty-five.
Now money. A restaurant bill of forty-eight dollars, and you want to tip fifteen percent. Ten percent is one tenth, so the decimal point moves one place. Four dollars eighty.
Five percent is half of that. Two dollars forty. Together, seven dollars twenty.
And twenty percent is the tenth, doubled.
Your turn. Fifteen percent of sixty dollars?
A tenth is six dollars. Half of that is three. Nine dollars.
Now a stranger one. What's eight percent of twenty-five dollars?
Turn it round. Twenty-five percent of eight dollars is a quarter of eight. Two dollars. That's the answer to both.

Percent means cents on the dollar. Eight cents from each of twenty-five dollars. Or twenty-five cents from each of eight. The same two hundred cents. The swap pays when one side is a friendly percent, like a half, a quarter or a tenth.
Some numbers are one step from a round one. Five is half of ten. So five times eighty-six is ten times eighty-six, cut in half. Eight hundred sixty, halved. Four hundred thirty.
The same cut works between two numbers. Fourteen times thirty-five. Halve the fourteen, double the thirty-five. Seven times seventy. Four hundred ninety.
Your turn. Sixteen times forty-five?
Halve and double. Eight times ninety. Seven hundred twenty. It pays when doubling makes a round number. One of them even, the other ending in five.
Prices sit just under a round number. Four things at nineteen dollars ninety-nine. Call it four twenties. Eighty dollars. Then give back four cents. Seventy-nine dollars ninety-six. Round, then fix.
Your turn. Three things at four dollars ninety-nine each?
Three fives are fifteen dollars. Give back three cents. Fourteen dollars ninety-seven. This one pays when the round number is a step or two away.
Forty-seven times fifty-three. Before you start on the parts, look at the two numbers. What number sits exactly halfway between them?
Fifty. One is three below it, the other three above.
So draw fifty squared, and lay the rectangle over it. It sticks out by three at the top, and falls short by three at the side.
Move the part that sticks out into the gap. It nearly fills it. What's missing is one small square, three by three.
So the answer is fifty squared, minus three squared. Twenty-five hundred, minus nine. Two thousand four hundred ninety-one.
Your turn. Nineteen times twenty-one?
The middle is twenty, and they're one away. Four hundred, minus one. Three hundred ninety-nine.
It needs a middle that's easy to square, and a small distance. Forty-seven times fifty-six has its middle at fifty-one and a half. Back to parts.

The next trick comes with a story. Los Alamos, in the nineteen forties, where the first atomic bomb was being built. Hans Bethe runs the theory division, and Richard Feynman works for him. They're putting numbers into a formula, and they get to forty-eight squared.
Feynman reaches for the calculator. Bethe says it's twenty-three hundred.
Feynman starts pushing the buttons anyway. And Bethe says that if he wants it exactly, it's twenty-three oh four.
Feynman is impressed. And Bethe asks him a question. Don't you know how to square numbers near fifty?
Fifty squared is twenty-five hundred. How would you get from there to forty-eight squared?
Bethe's way. Forty-eight is two below fifty, so take two hundred off. That's his twenty-three hundred. Then add two squared. Twenty-three oh four.
Here's the picture, and it's the move from before. Forty-eight squared. Slice a strip off its side, two wide, and lay it along the top.
Now it's forty-six wide and fifty tall. Against fifty squared, it's short by four fifties. Two hundred. That's Bethe's twenty-three hundred.
And the end of the strip sticks out. Two by two. Plus four.
Now a number above fifty. What changes for fifty-three squared?

The same move. Slice off three, and lay it on top. Now it's fifty wide, and six taller than fifty squared. Six fifties. Three hundred. And the end sticks out, three by three. Nine. Two thousand eight hundred nine.
Which gives a quick way to say it. Start from twenty-five. Add the distance from fifty, or take it off. That's the hundreds. Then write the distance squared, as two digits. Nine is oh nine.
Your turn. Fifty-two squared?
Twenty-five plus two is twenty-seven. Two squared is four. Oh four. Twenty-seven oh four.
Forty-six squared?
Four below. Twenty-five minus four is twenty-one. Four squared is sixteen. Twenty-one sixteen.

That reads straight off while you're within nine of fifty. Further out, the distance squared has three digits, and it spills into the hundreds. Sixty-two squared is thirty-seven hundred, plus a hundred forty-four. Thirty-eight forty-four.
After that, Feynman says, he took up tricks like these himself. He says he very rarely beat Bethe to an answer. And he says what made it easy for Bethe. Every number was near something he knew.
Now they're mixed up, so the first job is to pick the trick. Pause whenever you like. A twenty percent tip on forty-five dollars?
Percent. A tenth is four dollars fifty. Doubled, nine dollars.
Seventy-five squared?
It ends in five. Seven times eight is fifty-six. Five thousand six hundred twenty-five. At the start, one like that took you longer than four seconds.
Six times forty-nine?
Round, then fix. Six fifties, less six. Two hundred ninety-four. Parts gets there too.
Forty-nine times fifty-one?
One either side of fifty. Twenty-five hundred, minus one. Two thousand four hundred ninety-nine.
Last one. Sixty-seven times seventy-eight?

Nothing to grab. No five, no easy middle, and the nearest round number doesn't make it easy. Parts still works. Sixty seventies, forty-two hundred. Sixty eights, forty-six eighty. Seven seventies, fifty-one seventy. Seven eights, fifty-two twenty-six.
That's four pieces with carrying, and it's slow. There's no shame in reaching for paper, or a calculator. That's what they're for.

But keep one habit even then. Round first. Seventy times eighty is fifty-six hundred. So if the screen says five hundred, or fifty thousand, you know a key was missed. It won't catch a wrong digit. It catches a wrong size.
One more, and it has a twist. Fifty-five squared?
It ends in five. Five times six is thirty, then twenty-five. And it's near fifty. Twenty-five plus five is thirty, then twenty-five. The same two numbers. That's no coincidence.

They're the same move. Slice a strip off a square, lay it along the top, and you have a rectangle and a small square. Thirty times forty, plus twenty-five. Forty-six times fifty, plus four. And fifty squared is forty-seven times fifty-three, plus nine.
In letters, it's the line from before, with one piece moved across.

And none of it takes a gift. It takes a few numbers you know well, and the habit of looking for the nearest one. Every number is near something you know. Sometimes that gives you the answer. It always gives you the size.
